title: Perform calf and heifer rearing, production and health care practices

lessons.title: Caring for the newborn calf
lessons.html:
Practical tasks at calving

This module is about doing the work with your own hands, safely and to standard. Your assessor will watch you perform each task.

Preparing the calving area

  • Clean, dry, well-bedded calving pen or a clean, sheltered camp near the dairy.
  • Calving kit ready: gloves, lubricant, clean calving ropes or chains, navel dip, towels, colostrum feeder, thermometer, record book.
  • Good light for night checks.

Watching a calving

  1. Check close-up cows regularly, day and night.
  2. Normal signs: restlessness, tail raised, water bag, then front feet and nose appearing.
  3. Call for help if there is no progress after a reasonable time, if you see only one leg, the tail, or the head without the legs, or if the cow is exhausted. Only trained people should assist; never pull with a tractor or bakkie.

Immediately after birth

  1. Clear mucus from the nose and mouth. Rub the calf with straw or a towel to stimulate breathing.
  2. Dip the whole navel in the farm's navel disinfectant.
  3. Feed colostrum as soon as possible, ideally within the first few hours. Feed the volume in the farm protocol by teat bottle; use a tube feeder only if trained.
  4. Tag the calf and record: dam number, calf number, date, sex, birth difficulty, colostrum given and by whom.
  5. Move the calf to a clean, dry, individual pen.

Testing colostrum

Use a Brix refractometer or colostrometer if the farm has one. Put a few drops of colostrum on the refractometer glass, read the value and compare with the farm's standard for good colostrum. Store surplus good colostrum frozen in labelled bags; thaw in warm water, never in boiling water or a microwave, which damages antibodies.

Safety

Fresh cows can be protective of their calves. Keep a gate or barrier between you and the cow, and do not get trapped in a corner. Wear gloves during calving to protect against diseases such as brucellosis.

lessons.title: Feeding and managing calves to weaning
lessons.html:
Daily calf routine

  1. Check all calves before feeding. Note any that are dull, not standing, or scouring.
  2. Prepare milk or milk replacer: weigh powder, measure water at the temperature on the label, mix thoroughly.
  3. Feed the same amount, at the same temperature and times every day as the calf protocol says.
  4. Feed youngest first, sick calves last.
  5. Check that every calf drank its full feed. Record any that did not.
  6. Fill calf starter and water. Remove wet or stale starter.
  7. Wash buckets, teats and bottles in hot water with detergent, rinse and let them dry upside down.

Mixing milk replacer: example

If the label says 125 g of powder per litre of mix and you need 40 litres, you need 40 × 125 g = 5 000 g, or 5 kg of powder. Always use a scale or the measuring scoop provided; guessing causes scours.

Housing tasks

  • Add clean, dry bedding daily; replace wet bedding. Kneel test: if your knees get wet when you kneel, the bedding is too wet.
  • Check airflow without draughts at calf height.
  • Clean and disinfect pens between calves, and leave them empty to dry if possible.

Weaning

Wean calves according to the farm's criteria, usually based on daily starter intake. Reduce milk over the time set in the protocol. Keep weaned calves in small groups of similar size and continue to watch them closely for the first weeks.

Routine procedures

Disbudding, removal of extra teats and vaccinations are done by trained persons following the vet's plan, with pain relief as the vet advises. Hold calves gently and firmly; never lift calves by the tail or ears.

lessons.title: Calf health checks and heifer care
lessons.html:
Doing a health check

Use a simple scoring routine for every calf, every day:

CheckNormalReport if
AttitudeAlert, gets up to feedDull, slow, will not stand
AppetiteDrinks full feedLeaves milk, slow to drink
DungFirm to softWatery, bloody, smelly
Eyes and noseBright, cleanSunken eyes, discharge
BreathingQuiet, evenFast, coughing, head tilt
NavelDry, smallSwollen, hot, wet
TemperatureIn the normal range on the farm chartAbove or below the range

Take temperature with a digital rectal thermometer, cleaning it between calves. Report sick calves immediately. Give oral electrolytes and treatments only as instructed by the supervisor or vet, and record everything, including withdrawal dates.

Heifer tasks

  • Weighing: weigh heifers on the scale or with a weigh band, record the weight and compare with the growth chart.
  • Body condition scoring: score heifers regularly; report heifers that are too thin or too fat.
  • Parasite control: deworm and apply tick control according to the vet's plan and product labels, wearing gloves and protective equipment.
  • Heat detection and breeding: observe heats, record them, and present heifers for AI or bull service at the right time.
  • Pregnancy checks: assist the vet by moving heifers calmly into the crush.
  • Pre-calving: move in-calf heifers to the close-up group as planned and train them in the parlour.

Working in a crush

Never put your arm through the crush bars in front of a moving animal. Close the head clamp and back bar before working. Keep one person in charge of the gate.

Key points

  • Prepare the calving area and kit before calving starts.
  • Clear the airway, dip the navel, feed colostrum and record every birth.
  • Mix milk replacer exactly and wash feeding equipment after every feed.
  • Check every calf daily and report sick calves at once.
  • Weigh and condition-score heifers and work safely in the crush.
